units.grammar: SIMPLE, CONTINUOUS OR PERFECT. Present perfect (have/has + past participle): past events with no finished time given, often with just, already, yet, ever, never, since, for. 'I've already seen that film.' Past simple: finished actions at a stated past time. 'We moved here in 2019.' Past perfect (had + past participle): something that happened before another past moment. 'When I arrived, the bus had left.'
existing_questions_sample: I ____ (never / try) sushi before, so I'm a bit nervous. | have never tried
We ____ (move) to Valencia in 2019. | moved
When we got to the cinema, the film ____ (already / start). | had already started
Be quiet! The baby ____ (sleep). | is sleeping
My sister ____ (always / take) my charger without asking. It's so annoying! | is always taking
While I ____ (wait) for the bus, it started to snow. | was waiting
Correct it: I have seen Marta yesterday. | I saw Marta yesterday.
She ____ her homework yet. (hasn't finished / didn't finish) | hasn't finished
It was the first time he ____ (fly) in a helicopter. | had flown
This is the second time I ____ (lose) my keys this week. | have lost
They ____ here since 2020. (live / have lived / lived) | have lived
Correct it: What do you do right now? | What are you doing right now?

units.grammar: PRESENT PERFECT SIMPLE AND CONTINUOUS. Both tenses link the past to now, without saying exactly when something happened. Present perfect simple: a finished action with a result now, or how many / how often. 'I've written two emails.' Present perfect continuous (have/has been + -ing): focus on the activity or how long, maybe unfinished. 'I've been writing emails all morning.'
existing_questions_sample: I ____ (read) three chapters so far today. | have read
Your eyes are red. ____ (you / cry)? | Have you been crying
She ____ that novel. You can borrow it now. (has finished / has been finishing) | has finished
We ____ (wait) for forty minutes and the bus still isn't here. | have been waiting
I ____ English for six years. (am learning / have been learning) | have been learning
How many times ____ (you / visit) London? | have you visited
I ____ (know) Pablo since primary school. | have known
Correct it: I've been having this bike for years. | I've had this bike for years.
He's out of breath because he ____ (run). | has been running
They ____ (win) five matches this season. | have won
How long ____ (it / rain)? | has it been raining
I ____ my phone. Can you help me look for it? (have lost / have been losing) | have lost

units.grammar: THE GRAMMAR OF PHRASAL VERBS. A phrasal verb is a verb + one or two particles (adverb or preposition). The meaning is often not literal: 'give up' = stop trying. Some have no object: 'The plane took off late.' Verb + adverb + object: a noun object can go before or after the particle ('turn off the TV' / 'turn the TV off'), but a pronoun must go in the middle: 'turn it off'.
existing_questions_sample: Replace the noun with a pronoun: Turn off the radio. | Turn it off.
Correct it: I'll look the children after. | I'll look after the children.
That music is too loud. Please ____. (turn down it / turn it down) | turn it down
Can you ____ while I'm away? (look my cat after / look after my cat) | look after my cat
Replace the noun with a pronoun: She gave back the books. | She gave them back.
I'm really looking forward ____ the concert. (to / at / for) | to
Correct it: We've run milk out of. | We've run out of milk.
Replace the noun with a pronoun: He takes after his father. | He takes after him.
I don't know this word. I'll ____. (look up it / look it up) | look it up
My car broke ____ on the motorway. (down / off / out) | down
Correct it: She gets on her cousins with. | She gets on with her cousins.
Replace the noun with a pronoun: Pick up your clothes! | Pick them up!

units.unit_title: MODALS (1): NECESSITY, OBLIGATION, PROHIBITION AND ADVICE
units.grammar: MODALS (1): NECESSITY, OBLIGATION, PROHIBITION AND ADVICE. need to = it is necessary; don't need to / needn't = it isn't necessary. 'You need to book early.' must: the speaker feels it is obligatory. have to: the rule comes from outside. 'I must call Gran.' 'We have to wear a uniform.' mustn't = it is forbidden. don't have to = it's optional. They are very different! 'You mustn't run here.' 'You don't have to come.'
vocab: go over and over (sth) in your mind
existing_questions_sample: You ____ touch that wire. It's dangerous! (mustn't / don't have to) | mustn't
Tomorrow is a holiday, so we ____ get up early. (mustn't / don't have to) | don't have to
You look tired. You ____ go to bed earlier. (should / mustn't) | should
Correct it: You ought see a doctor. | You ought to see a doctor.
In my school, students ____ wear a uniform. It's a rule. (have to / should) | have to
Correct it: She musts finish it today. | She must finish it today.
Past of must: Yesterday I ____ stay late at school. | had to
You ____ bring food. There's plenty here. (needn't / mustn't) | needn't
Correct it: He don't have to come. | He doesn't have to come.
You ____ eat so many sweets. They're bad for your teeth. (shouldn't / don't have to) | shouldn't
Complete with one word: You ought ____ apologise to her. | to
Passengers ____ smoke anywhere on the plane. (mustn't / needn't) | mustn't

units.grammar: PRESENT AND PAST HABITS. Present habits: present simple + frequency adverb (before the main verb, after be) or a frequency phrase at the end. 'I hardly ever eat meat.' 'We meet from time to time.' always / constantly / continually + present continuous shows a habit annoys you: 'She's always borrowing my pens.' used to + infinitive: past habits and states that are no longer true. Negative and question: didn't use to / Did you use to ...?
existing_questions_sample: When I was little, I ____ be afraid of dogs. (used to / use to) | used to
Correct it: I didn't used to like olives. | I didn't use to like olives.
We ____ a house by the sea when I was a child. (used to have / would have) | used to have
He ____ (always / lose) his keys! It drives me mad. | is always losing
Put the adverb in the right place: She is late. (never) | She is never late.
Put the adverb in the right place: I eat meat. (rarely) | I rarely eat meat.
Every summer, Grandad ____ us fishing. (would take / was used to take) | would take
Nowadays I ____ running twice a week. (go / use to go) | go
____ (you / use) play with dolls when you were small? | Did you use to
My old neighbours ____ (constantly / shout) at each other. It was awful. | were constantly shouting
I ____ in ghosts when I was six. (would believe / used to believe) | used to believe
We see each other once ____ a while. (in / on / at) | in

units.grammar: BE/GET USED TO. be used to + noun or -ing: something is normal for you now. 'I'm used to the noise.' get used to + noun or -ing: something is slowly becoming normal. 'I'm getting used to my new school.' Here 'to' is a preposition, so the next verb takes -ing: 'She's used to cooking for ten people.' (NOT 'used to cook') be and get can go in any tense: 'I wasn't used to it', 'You'll get used to it', 'He has got used to it'.
existing_questions_sample: I'm used to ____ (get) up early, so 6 a.m. is no problem. | getting
It took me months to ____ used to the cold weather. (be / get) | get
She's used to ____ on the left. (drive / driving) | driving
When I was five, I ____ have a toy rabbit. (used to / was used to) | used to
Don't worry, you'll soon ____ used to your new school. (get / getting) | get
He has lived in Seville for years, so he ____ the heat. (is used to / used to) | is used to
I can't get used to ____ (wear) glasses. | wearing
Correct it: I'm not use to spicy food. | I'm not used to spicy food.
We ____ live in a flat, but now we have a house. (used to / are used to) | used to
She still hasn't ____ (get) used to her new timetable. | got
Are you used to ____ (speak) in public? | speaking
At first the noise bothered us, but we slowly ____ used to it. (got / were) | got

units.grammar: NARRATIVE TENSES. Past simple tells the main events of a story in order: 'She opened the box and smiled.' Past continuous sets the scene or shows an action in progress: 'The wind was blowing hard.' Past perfect simple (had + past participle): a completed action before another past event. 'By the time we arrived, they had eaten.'
existing_questions_sample: When I got home, my brother ____ (already / eat) all the pizza. | had already eaten
Her eyes were red because she ____ (cry). | had been crying
We ____ (walk) for three hours when we finally saw the village. | had been walking
I opened the door, ____ (switch) on the light and screamed. | switched
The sun ____ (shine) when we left the house. | was shining
I didn't recognise him because he ____ (grow) a beard. | had grown
By the time the police arrived, the thief ____. (escaped / had escaped) | had escaped
Correct it: I had been knowing her for years. | I had known her for years.
While they ____ (sleep), someone stole their car. | were sleeping
The ground was wet. It ____ (rain) all night. | had been raining
She ____ three emails before lunch. (had written / had been writing) | had written
He was nervous because he ____ (never / fly) before. | had never flown

units.grammar: FUTURE (1): REVIEW. Present simple for timetables and fixed schedules: 'My flight leaves at noon.' Present continuous for arrangements with other people: 'I'm seeing the dentist on Friday.' be going to: intentions already decided, and predictions from what you can see now. 'It's going to fall!' will: decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers, promises and predictions based on opinion. 'I'll carry that for you.'
existing_questions_sample: The train ____ (leave) at 6.45 tomorrow morning. | leaves
Look at those black clouds! It ____ rain. (is going to / will) | is going to
'The phone's ringing.' 'OK, ____ it.' (I'll answer / I'm answering) | I'll answer
I'll text you as soon as I ____ (arrive). | arrive
We'll start when everyone ____ here. (is / will be) | is
Hurry up! The film is ____ to start. (about / soon) | about
I ____ (meet) Laura at five tomorrow. We booked a table. | am meeting
I promise I ____ (not / tell) anyone your secret. | won't tell
She has decided: she ____ study medicine. (is going to / will) | is going to
Don't go out until you ____ your homework. (finish / will finish) | finish
What time ____ (the concert / start) on Saturday? | does the concert start
I think Spain ____ (win) the next World Cup. | will win

units.grammar: FUTURE (2): CONTINUOUS AND PERFECT. Future continuous (will be + -ing): an action in progress at a future moment. 'At ten tomorrow I'll be sitting my exam.' It is also a polite way to ask about plans: 'Will you be using the computer later?' Future perfect (will have + past participle): an action finished before a future moment, often with by. 'By Friday I'll have read the book.'
existing_questions_sample: This time next week, I ____ (lie) on a beach. | will be lying
By 2030, I ____ (finish) university. | will have finished
By June, she ____ (study) English for ten years. | will have been studying
Don't call at nine. We ____ (have) dinner then. | will be having
By the time you arrive, the film ____. (will be starting / will have started) | will have started
I'll have ____ it by Friday. (finish / finished) | finished
At midnight tonight, I ____ (sleep). | will be sleeping
____ (you / use) the car tonight? I'd like to borrow it. | Will you be using
Next month my parents ____ (be) married for twenty years. | will have been
At this moment tomorrow, we ____ over the Alps. (will be flying / will have flown) | will be flying
By the end of this year, he ____ (save) 1,000 euros. | will have saved
By 6 p.m. I ____ (work) for ten hours without a break. | will have been working

units.grammar: MODALS (2): MODALS IN THE PAST. would have + past participle: something imagined in the past that didn't really happen. 'You would have laughed!' should have / ought to have + past participle: criticism or regret about the past. 'I should have listened.' shouldn't have = it was a mistake to do it. needn't have + past participle: you did something, but it turned out to be unnecessary. 'You needn't have cooked; we'd already eaten.'
existing_questions_sample: You ____ (should / tell) me you were coming! I had no food ready. | should have told
I ____ (need / not / buy) milk; we already had three cartons. | needn't have bought
It was a holiday, so I ____ get up early. I stayed in bed. (didn't need to / needn't have) | didn't need to
I failed the test. I ____ (should / study) more. | should have studied
He ____ (should / not / shout) at her. She was only trying to help. | shouldn't have shouted
What a great party! You ____ (would / love) it. | would have loved
You should have ____ to bed earlier. (went / gone) | gone
I took an umbrella, but it didn't rain. I ____ (need / not / take) it. | needn't have taken
I'm glad I missed that film. I ____ (would / not / enjoy) it. | wouldn't have enjoyed
Complete with one word: She ought to ____ asked before borrowing my bike. | have
The museum was free, so we ____ pay. (didn't need to / shouldn't have) | didn't need to
Oh no, I'm soaked! I ____ (should / bring) a coat. | should have brought

units.grammar: RELATIVE CLAUSES. Defining clauses say which person or thing we mean. No commas. Use who/that for people, which/that for things: 'The boy who sits next to me is Dutch.' You can leave out who/which/that when it is the object of the clause: 'The film (that) we watched was long.' You can't when it is the subject.
existing_questions_sample: That's the girl ____ brother plays for Betis. (who / whose / which) | whose
This is the town ____ I was born. (which / where / that) | where
My mum, ____ is a nurse, works nights. (who / that) | who
The film ____ we saw last night was brilliant. (who / which / where) | which
Can the pronoun be left out? 'The book that I bought is great.' (yes / no) | yes
Can the pronoun be left out? 'The man who lives next door is a chef.' (yes / no) | no
Madrid, ____ is the capital of Spain, is very hot in summer. (which / that) | which
The boy ____ won the race is my cousin. (who / which / whose) | who
2015 was the year ____ we moved house. (when / where / whose) | when
Does this sentence need commas? 'My dad who is 50 loves skating.' (yes / no) | yes
Formal style: The person to ____ I spoke was helpful. (who / whom / which) | whom
He passed all his exams, ____ surprised everyone. (which / that / what) | which

units.grammar: THE PASSIVE (1): REVIEW. Form the passive with be in the right tense + past participle: 'The bridge was built in 1990.' 'Dinner is being cooked.' Use it when the doer is unknown, obvious or unimportant, or when you want to focus on the thing affected: 'My bike has been stolen.' Add the doer with by only when it matters: 'The song was written by a teenager.' Verbs with two objects can make the person the subject: 'She was given a prize.'
existing_questions_sample: This castle ____ (build) in the twelfth century. | was built
Be careful! The floor ____ (clean) right now. | is being cleaned
My wallet ____ (steal)! I can't find it anywhere. | has been stolen
The results ____ (announce) tomorrow morning. | will be announced
Make it passive: Someone broke the window. The window ____. | was broken
'Don Quixote' was written ____ Cervantes. (by / from / for) | by
When we arrived, the room ____ (already / decorate). | had already been decorated
I don't cut my own hair. I ____ it cut at the hairdresser's. (have / make) | have
She got her laptop ____ (fix) at a shop in town. | fixed
English is ____ all over the world. (spoke / spoken / speaking) | spoken
Make it passive: They are repairing the road. The road ____. | is being repaired
We're going to ____ the house painted next month. (have / be) | have

units.grammar: THE PASSIVE (2): OTHER STRUCTURES. Passive infinitive = (to) be + past participle. It follows verbs like want, hope, expect, seem: 'Everyone wants to be liked.' Verb + object + passive infinitive: 'We expect the work to be finished soon.' After modal verbs there is no to: 'Phones must be switched off.' -ing passive = being + past participle, after verbs like enjoy, avoid, hate, remember, don't mind: 'I hate being told what to do.'
existing_questions_sample: Nobody likes ____ (criticise) in public. | being criticised
He hopes ____ (choose) for the school team. | to be chosen
All phones must ____ (switch) off during the exam. | be switched
I remember ____ (take) to the zoo when I was four. | being taken
She insisted on ____ (tell) the truth by her friends. | being told
The teacher expects the projects ____ (hand) in on Friday. | to be handed
I don't mind ____ what to do. (to be told / being told) | being told
This door should ____ locked at night. (be / to be / being) | be
The cat wants ____ (feed). | to be fed
He's tired of ____ (treat) like a child. | being treated
She seems ____ by everyone. (to be liked / being liked) | to be liked
The thief managed to avoid ____ (catch). | being caught

units.grammar: REPORTED SPEECH. When the reporting verb is in the past, the tense usually moves one step back: 'I'm tired' -> She said she was tired. will -> would, can -> could, past simple / present perfect -> past perfect. No change is needed when the reporting verb is in the present ('He says he likes it'), or when the fact is still true or still in the future.
existing_questions_sample: 'I'm hungry.' -> He said he ____ hungry. | was
'I'll help you.' -> She said she ____ help me. | would
'I can swim.' -> He said he ____ swim. | could
'We have finished.' -> They said they ____ finished. | had
'Where do you live?' -> She asked me where I ____. | lived
He asked me where ____. (was the station / the station was) | the station was
'Do you like jazz?' -> He asked me ____ I liked jazz. (if / that / what) | if
'Sit down!' -> The teacher told us ____ down. | to sit
'Don't touch it!' -> She told me ____ it. | not to touch
'I like this song.' -> She says she ____ this song. (likes / liked) | likes
'I saw him yesterday.' -> She said she had seen him the day ____. | before
She ____ me that she was leaving. (said / told) | told

units.grammar: MODALS (3): DEDUCTION. must + verb: you feel sure something is true. 'They look identical. They must be twins.' can't / couldn't + verb: you feel sure something is NOT true. (Don't use mustn't for this.) 'That can't be right.' may / might / could + verb: it is possible. may not / might not = perhaps not. 'She might be at the gym.'
existing_questions_sample: He's been running for hours. He ____ be exhausted. (must / can't) | must
That ____ be Ana. She's in Paris this week. (must / can't) | can't
I'm not sure where Leo is. He ____ be in the library. (might / must) | might
The ground is wet. It ____ (must / rain) last night. | must have rained
She ____ (can't / see) us; she walked straight past. | can't have seen
They're late. They ____ (might / miss) the bus. | might have missed
The lights are off. He ____ be at home. (mustn't / can't) | can't
You ____ have been tired after that 20-kilometre walk! (must / can't) | must
I can hear a violin. She must ____. (practise / be practising) | be practising
He ____ (can't / finish) already! He only started five minutes ago. | can't have finished
Take an umbrella. It ____ rain later. (could / must) | could
Complete with one word: They might not ____ received my email. | have

units.grammar: CONDITIONALS (1): REVIEW. Zero conditional: if / when + present, present. For things that are always true. 'If you press this, the screen turns on.' First conditional: if + present, will / can / might + verb. A real future possibility. 'If I see her, I'll tell her.' unless = if ... not. Second conditional: if + past simple, would / could / might + verb. Imaginary or unlikely present or future. 'If I were you, I'd apologise.'
existing_questions_sample: If you heat ice, it ____ (melt). | melts
If it rains tomorrow, we ____ (stay) at home. | will stay
If I ____ (be) you, I'd tell the truth. | were
If I had more free time, I ____ (learn) the guitar. | would learn
If she had studied, she ____ (pass) the exam. | would have passed
If we ____ (leave) earlier, we wouldn't have missed the train. | had left
If I ____ him, I'll tell him. (see / will see) | see
You won't pass ____ you work harder. (unless / if) | unless
What would you do if you ____ (win) the lottery? | won
If I ____ about the party, I would have come. (knew / had known) | had known
Plants die if they ____ (not / get) enough water. | don't get
If he ____ so shy, he would talk to her. (wasn't / hadn't been) | wasn't

units.grammar: CONDITIONALS (2): MIXED. Mixed conditionals join two different times in one sentence. Past condition -> present result: if + past perfect, would / could / might + verb. 'If I had slept more, I wouldn't be tired now.' Present or general condition -> past result: if + past simple, would have + past participle. 'If I spoke French, I would have understood the film.'
existing_questions_sample: If I had eaten breakfast, I ____ (not / be) hungry now. | wouldn't be
If she weren't so lazy, she ____ (finish) the project last week. | would have finished
If we ____ (take) the map, we wouldn't be lost now. | had taken
If he ____ (speak) German, he would have got that job in Berlin. | spoke
If I had saved money, I ____ a new phone now. (would have / would have had) | would have
If you weren't afraid of flying, you ____ with us last summer. (would come / would have come) | would have come
If they had left on time, they ____ (be) here by now. | would be
If I ____ (not / forget) my keys, I wouldn't be standing outside now. | hadn't forgotten
Present or past result? 'If I'd studied medicine, I'd be a doctor.' (present / past) | present
If I ____ (know) how to cook, I would have made you dinner yesterday. | knew
If you had listened to me, we ____ (not / be) in this mess now. | wouldn't be
If she ____ the bus, she would be here now. (didn't miss / hadn't missed) | hadn't missed

units.grammar: USES OF VERB + -ING. Some verbs are followed by -ing, not the infinitive: enjoy, avoid, deny, admit, consider, suggest, finish, mind, keep, imagine, risk. 'She keeps texting me.' After a preposition the verb is always -ing: 'good at drawing', 'without asking', 'after leaving school'. Set expressions take -ing: it's not worth, there's no point, can't help, have difficulty, spend time, be fed up with. 'There's no point complaining.'
existing_questions_sample: She suggested ____ (go) to the beach. | going
He left without ____ (say) goodbye. | saying
It's not worth ____ (wait) any longer. | waiting
I can't help ____ when he sings. (to laugh / laughing) | laughing
____ (eat) too much sugar is bad for you. | Eating
I'm fed up with ____ (do) the same exercises. | doing
Because she felt ill, she went home. = ____ ill, she went home. | Feeling
He denied ____ the window. (to break / breaking) | breaking
We spent the whole afternoon ____ (play) video games. | playing
____ (not / know) the answer, I stayed quiet. | Not knowing
Are you good at ____ (draw)? | drawing
Correct it: I've finished to read the book. | I've finished reading the book.

units.grammar: SUBJECT–VERB AGREEMENT. Some nouns end in -s but are singular: news, maths, physics, politics, athletics, gymnastics, the United States. 'Politics is complicated.' everyone, someone, anybody, nobody, etc. take a singular verb, but we refer back with they / their: 'Someone has left their bag.' When a clause or an -ing phrase is the subject, the verb is singular: 'Making new friends takes time.'
existing_questions_sample: The news ____ really bad today. (is / are) | is
Everybody ____ (know) the answer to that. | knows
One of my friends ____ (live) in Ireland. | lives
Both of my sisters ____ (play) the piano. | play
Maths ____ my favourite subject. (is / are) | is
Learning languages ____ (take) a lot of time. | takes
Correct it: Nobody like getting up early. | Nobody likes getting up early.
A lot of the water ____ polluted. (is / are) | is
A lot of people ____ (think) the same. | think
The United States ____ fifty states. (has / have) | has
Someone has left ____ umbrella here. (their / its) | their
Most of my friends ____ (not / like) horror films. | don't like

units.grammar: DETERMINERS. the: for something unique, something specific we both know about, or something already mentioned. 'I bought a cake. The cake was delicious.' a / an: with a singular countable noun when it is one of many or mentioned for the first time. 'She's got a new bike.' No article: plural and uncountable nouns when we speak in general. 'Dogs need exercise.' 'Sugar is bad for your teeth.'
existing_questions_sample: I saw ____ great film last night. (a / the / no article) | a
____ sun rises in the east. (A / The) | The
I love ____ music. It's my whole life. (a / the / no article) | no article
We don't have ____ time, so hurry up! (much / many) | much
How ____ students are there in your class? (much / many) | many
I've got ____ friends here, so I'm never lonely. (few / a few) | a few
He has ____ money, so he can't afford a holiday. (little / a little) | little
I bought a jacket and a hat. ____ jacket was expensive. (A / The) | The
There's ____ of food for everyone. (plenty / several) | plenty
She gave me ____ good advice. (a / some) | some
We visited ____ museums in Rome. (several / a little) | several
Could I have ____ bit of cake, please? (a / the / some) | a
